title: UX Design Fundamentals
summary: Learn user experience design: the design process, user research and personas, information architecture and wireframes, usability heuristics, accessible design and usability testing with real metrics.
audience: Aspiring designers, developers, product managers and entrepreneurs building apps and websites

body.p: User experience (UX) design shapes how people feel and succeed when they use a product: an app, website, form, ATM or even a clinic's appointment process. UI (user interface) design is one part of it, covering the visual and interactive surface. UX also covers research, structure, content, accessibility and testing.

steps: Understand: research users, their goals, context and frustrations.
Define: turn findings into clear problems and requirements.
Prototype: build quick versions, from paper sketches to clickable mock-ups.
Test: watch real users try the prototype, then improve and repeat.

body.p: The process is iterative: each round of testing feeds the next design. Teams that test early fix problems when changes are cheap, rather than after launch when they are expensive.

list: Many users are on low-cost phones with small screens and limited data.
Connections can be slow or drop; save progress and keep pages light.
Users may read in a second language; use plain words.
Some share devices or use them in bright sunlight; consider privacy and contrast.

body.tip: You are not your user. Even experienced designers are regularly surprised by what real users do.

body.p: Research reveals what people actually need. Methods include interviews, observation in context, surveys, analytics and reviewing support tickets. Qualitative methods (interviews, observation) explain why; quantitative methods (surveys, analytics) show how many.

list: Ask about past behaviour: "Tell me about the last time you paid a bill on your phone."
Avoid leading questions such as "Wouldn't it be great if…?"
Listen more than you talk, and ask "why?" and "can you show me?"
Interview a range of users, including less confident ones.
Get consent and protect personal data.
Personas: short, evidence-based profiles of key user types, with goals and frustrations.
Journey maps: the steps a user takes, with feelings and pain points at each step.
Problem statements: "Market traders need to record daily sales quickly because they have little time between customers."

body.tip: Base personas on real research, not imagination; a persona nobody can trace to evidence just repeats the team's assumptions.

body.p: Information architecture (IA) organises and labels content so people can find things. Good IA uses the words users use, groups related items, and keeps navigation shallow and predictable. Card sorting, in which users group topics on cards, shows how they expect content to be organised.

Wireframes are simple layouts showing where content and controls go, without colour or final images. They let teams agree on structure quickly. Start with paper or simple digital boxes, then build clickable prototypes to test flows.

list: Visual hierarchy: the most important item is the most prominent.
One primary action per screen, clearly labelled with a verb ("Pay now").
Group related items and align them to a grid.
Design for small screens first, then expand for larger ones.
Keep forms short: ask only what you need, label every field and show errors next to the field.

body.tip: Use real content in wireframes as early as possible; dummy Latin filler text hides labels that are too long or unclear.

body.p: Usability heuristics are rules of thumb for spotting problems. Jakob Nielsen's ten heuristics are widely used:

list: Visibility of system status: show what is happening (loading, saved, sent).
Match the real world: use familiar words and concepts.
User control and freedom: allow undo and cancel.
Consistency and standards: similar things look and work alike.
Error prevention: stop mistakes before they happen, for example by confirming large payments.
Recognition rather than recall: show options instead of making people remember them.
Flexibility and efficiency: shortcuts for experienced users.
Aesthetic and minimalist design: remove clutter that competes with what matters.
Help users recognise, diagnose and recover from errors: plain-language messages with a solution.
Help and documentation: easy to find and focused on tasks.

body.p: A heuristic evaluation, in which several reviewers check a design against these principles, finds many problems cheaply, but it complements testing with real users rather than replacing it.

body.tip: Rewrite every error message to say what happened and how to fix it: "Phone number must have 10 digits" beats "Invalid input".

body.p: Accessible design lets people with disabilities use products: blind users with screen readers, people with low vision or colour blindness, people with motor impairments using keyboards or switches, and deaf users who need captions. It also helps everyone: older users, people in bright sun or using a phone one-handed.

list: Text contrast: at least 4.5 : 1 for normal text. Black on white is 21 : 1; mid-grey #767676 on white is about 4.54 : 1 and just passes; light grey #999999 on white is only about 2.85 : 1 and fails.
Do not rely on colour alone; add labels or icons.
Give images meaningful alternative text.
Make everything usable with a keyboard, with a visible focus outline.
Use real headings, labels and buttons so screen readers can navigate.
Make touch targets large enough, and caption videos.

body.p: Many countries require accessibility for public services, and accessible products reach more customers.

body.tip: Try your design with the screen zoomed to 200% and with only a keyboard. Both tests reveal many problems in minutes.

body.p: In a usability test, a participant tries realistic tasks with a prototype or product while the facilitator watches and asks them to think aloud. The goal is to observe problems, not to get opinions about colours.

Small rounds work well. A classic model assumes each user reveals about 31% of the problems; five users would then reveal about 1 - (1 - 0.31)⁵, roughly 84%. It is usually better to test five users, fix the issues and test again than to test fifteen users once.

list: Task success rate: 18 of 20 participants completing a payment is 90%.
Time on task and number of errors.

System Usability Scale (SUS): a 10-question survey. For odd items subtract 1 from the answer (1 to 5); for even items subtract the answer from 5; add them and multiply by 2.5. Answers 4, 2, 5, 1, 4, 2, 4, 2, 5, 2 give a score of 82.5, well above the commonly cited average of about 68.
After launch: analytics, conversion rates, support tickets and A/B tests.

body.tip: Write tasks as goals, not instructions: "Send R200 to your sister", not "Tap the Send button".

quiz.q: How does UX differ from UI?
options: UX covers the whole experience; UI is the visual and interactive surface
UI includes research and UX does not

quiz.q: Why is the design process iterative?
options: It removes the need for prototypes
Testing reveals problems to fix in the next round
Tell me about the last time you paid a bill on your phone
Wouldn't you love our new feature?
Our app is easy, isn't it?
Do you agree the old app is bad?

quiz.q: A persona should be based on:
What does card sorting help with?
options: Organising content the way users expect
A simple layout showing structure without final visuals

quiz.q: "Show a loading indicator while a payment processes" follows which heuristic?
Which is the better error message?
What minimum contrast does WCAG require for normal text?

Why not rely on colour alone to show errors?
options: Colour-blind users may not see the difference
